name: CEARCH (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Moves money: the grants it made and advised, and the funding its research informed, are valued at global health charities read live, which bring their own countries.
summary: CEARCH (the Centre for Exploratory Altruism Research) researches neglected causes, mostly in global health, then makes and advises grants to the best projects it finds and does research commissioned by funders. We count its running costs from its launch in October 2022 to May 2025 against what it moved: $213,000 of grants to salt-reduction and soda-tax policy projects made with the donors it advises, and the funding its commissioned research changed. Both are valued at the global-health portfolio (GiveWell's Top Charities), live, net of where the money would otherwise have gone. At the defaults it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000; the result is mostly uncertainty in its running costs, which it doesn't publish, and in how much its research changed funders' decisions, both our judgments. The funding its research changed is discounted for missing data.

sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

source.title: Charity Entrepreneurship, Centre for Exploratory Altruism Research (profile, archived 20 January 2025)

rows.explainer: Our judgment: CEARCH publishes no accounts (its financials page was taken down, and its fiscal sponsor's return doesn't break it out). Its incubator's profile, as archived in January 2025, gives a $100,000 seed grant, $262,000 raised to date and a team of two. Less the $100,000 ACX Grants gave it in February 2024 to regrant to nutrition charities (counted as money moved below, not running costs), that is about $260,000 over the 27 months from October 2022: about $116,000 a year, or $161,000 if the ACX money paid running costs. It fits about one and a half full-time staff (its founder full time, part-time research fellows) at a newly incubated organisation's pay, with consultants and the sponsor's fee. $120,000 a year, from $70,000 to $170,000.

rows.explainer: CEARCH's whole running costs a year: a fiscally sponsored project with no accounts of its own.

rows.explainer: 0: CEARCH works through the money it moves and the decisions its research informs, counted below. Its published research also fed Ambitious Impact's top charity ideas (salt reduction in 2024, soda taxes in 2026), but no charity was launched from them by May 2025, so no outcome of that is counted; the side-effects row takes it in.

rows.label: Grants made with the donors it advises: salt reduction policy, to May 2025 (US$)

source.title: Joel Tan (CEARCH), comment on CEARCH's Deep Report on Hypertension (EA Forum, 26 May 2025)
source.quote: In hypertension/salt reduction policy, CEARCH (in collaboration with the donors we advise) has made 150k in grants

rows.explainer: Grants CEARCH made with the donors it advises to projects that press for, and help governments carry out, rules to cut the salt in food. Its Top Giving Recommendations page names ImagineLaw (the Philippines) among the groups it recommends and funds; neither it nor the Global Health Advocacy Incubator (soda taxes) has a model here, so a dollar is valued at the global-health portfolio (GiveWell's Top Charities, weighted by its funds).

rows.label: Grants made: enforcement of soda taxes, to May 2025 (US$)

source.title: Joel Tan (CEARCH), comment on CEARCH's Deep Report on Hypertension (EA Forum, 26 May 2025)
source.quote: In diabetes/soda taxes, CEARCH has made 63k in grants

rows.explainer: Grants for technical help to enforce taxes on sugary drinks, one pooled grant of its founder and five other donors.

rows.label: Share of those grants made only because of CEARCH
rows.explainer: No survey of the donors it advises: the site's shared figure for a meta charity without one (@meta.own_effect_share). For context: the grants came out of CEARCH's own grant rounds (16 projects evaluated in five rounds from 2023 to 2026, four funded: its Global Health Policy Fund report, https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ItDaNb7rnW0GNZUvUnCSu4tQbyDpL1CF9s-zEYStk3w) and its regranting budget, so the projects were found and chosen by it; but part of the money is its founder's own giving and that of donors who give to policy projects in any case, who could have found the same groups (the salt-reduction groups it backs are known to other funders). Whether the money would otherwise have been given at all is the shared new-money share below.

rows.label: Money moved a year (US$)
rows.explainer: The grants made to May 2025, the share CEARCH caused, per year of the period. No other grants are published: its global catastrophic risk proposals found no donor (May 2025), the mental health funding it advised is in the funding its commissions changed; its grant rounds after May 2025 (four projects funded over five rounds to 2026) give no amounts. Advice to other grantmakers is in the funding changed below.

rows.label: Commissioned research projects in the period

source.title: CEARCH, Commissioned Research
source.quote: Some areas we have researched for partners include advanced market commitments, childhood vaccinations, salt reduction policy, mental health

rows.explainer: Our judgment. CEARCH names seven areas it researched for funders (advance market commitments, childhood vaccinations, salt reduction policy, mental health, the meta funding landscape, sleep apnea, female genital mutilation), for funders including the Flourishing Minds Fund and Coppice Philanthropy; the mental health report came out in January 2024. The meta funding landscape report (for Meta Charity Funders) is left out: its funders' money goes to organisations that raise or direct money, not to the global health work the funding is valued at. Not all fell before May 2025, and a consultation (its fund report says GiveWell and Charity Entrepreneurship have consulted its founder) isn't a commission. 4, from 2 to 7.

rows.label: Funding a commissioned project informs (US$)

source.title: Meta Charity Funders, Second round retrospective (EA Forum)

rows.explainer: Our judgment: the grant money a commissioning funder decides on with the report in hand. Its clients are small funders and funding circles; as a reference class, the funding circle that commissioned its meta report granted $687,000, $2.04 million and $363,000 in its first three rounds, across all its areas. A commission informs one area's decisions, part of such a budget, over a year or two. $300,000, from $50,000 to $2 million.

rows.label: Share of that funding the research changed
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure for the share of advised money whose destination the advice changed, as for every meta charity without a survey of its clients (@meta.own_effect_share). A funder commissions a report because it is undecided, but decides with its own staff, advisers and priors.

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): the charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work.

rows.label: Value of a dollar all shifted (given anyway, now to a better use), at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: Money that would have been given or spent anyway counts only for the gain over where it would have gone: a grantmaker's grants, or spending that research or advice changed. Its owners spent it, so the organisation is credited its share of that gain (mobiliser_share).

rows.label: Value of the spending its research or advice changed (all shifted money), units of value
rows.explainer: Spending its research or advice changed, at a judged share of the money it informed: all of it would have been spent anyway, so it counts for the gain over where it would have gone, discounted for weak evidence and for an outcome not measured for this charity (docs/normalization.md 2.8, 2.12).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone. The donors gave it, so the organisation is credited its share of that good (mobiliser_share).

rows.label: Value of the career changes (units of value)
Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Our judgment, applied to the funding its commissioned research changed: the share of the gain counted that is real. A changed decision can be no better than the first plan, and commissioned work answers the client's question, which may not be the most valuable one. 0.7, from 0.4 to 0.9.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: what the funders would have done without CEARCH is netted out in the share of the grants it caused and the share of the funding its research changed (Convention 5: one question per adjustment).

rows.label: This charity's share among those who worked for the result
rows.explainer: 1: other advisers and the funders' own staff are netted out in the shares above, which count only the part CEARCH changed.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The skeleton's policy branch, unused here (0): its share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share (docs/normalization.md 2.24). The money moved and changed carry the mobiliser's share in their own rows.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin (the site's missing-data step, docs/normalization.md 2.12), for the funding its research changed: the projects and the money they inform are our judgment and the share changed the shared figure. The grants are CEARCH's own count, so the money moved takes no missing-data step.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above, for the empty policy branch.

rows.label: Side effects of its research beyond the money counted, as a share of its value

source.title: Ambitious Impact, Advocacy for salt intake reduction: AIM top idea 2024 (EA Forum)
source.quote: This investigation has greatly benefited from prior work by CEARCH

rows.explainer: Our judgment. Good not counted: its published reports fed Ambitious Impact's top charity ideas (salt reduction, 2024, which thanks it for extensive support; soda taxes, 2026), which Ambitious Impact tried to incubate in 2026, and donors who read its reports give in ways no one tracks. Harm: research can also steer money to weaker work where its estimates are optimistic, as its founder says its own figures may be up to three times too high. A fifth more, from nothing to three fifths.
